newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian communists threaten to fight liberal budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian communists threaten to fight liberal budget.

text.p: India's main communist party, a key member of the country's fractious ruling coalition, on Sunday served notice that it would fight some market-opening steps outlined in the federal budget.

Harkishen Singh Surjeet said his Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) would seek to reverse tax and import tariff cuts and a partial opening of the insurance market proposed by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in the budget.
"Taking an overall view I would say it is an elitist budget which is going to benefit the upper layer of the population," Surjeet, the CPI-M general secretary, told a private television channel.
A text of Surjeet's interview to Home TV, to be broadcast on Monday evening, was made available to Reuters.
Parliament will take up a crucial vote on the 1997/98 (April-March) budget later this month which is expected to test the stability of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's fragile 15-member coalition.
The CPI-M, which has 32 lawmakers in the 545-seat Lok Sabha or lower house of parliament, is a key coalition member but does not hold any cabinet posts.
The coalition commands a total of 178 votes in the Lok Sabha.

It survives because of support from the Congress party, which has 140 lawmakers. The Congress, which was ejected from power in national elections in May 1996, has also criticised some of the proposed tax cuts but signalled that it is not about to attempt to topple the government.

Chidambaram, in his February 28 budget proposals, slashed corporate and income taxes, cut import tariffs and provided a string of incentives to the capital markets in a bid to kick-start a dormant stockmarket and revive flagging investment.

If the budget proposals are approved by parliament, corporate tax on domestic firms will drop to 35 percent from 40 percent and on foreign firms to 48 percent from 55 percent. The peak customs tariffs will fall to 40 percent from 50 percent.
Chidambaram has also proposed cutting the top income-tax rate to 30 percent from 40 percent.

Surjeet said the communists would "raise our voice against the budget and what are its negative features" and oppose the planned steps in the Steering Committee, the ruling coalition's highest decision-making body.
The communist party was also opposed to the government's move on opening up of health insurance sector.

Chidambaram wants to allow private investors into pensions and health insurance by permitting joint ventures with its two state-run monopolies, Life Insurance Corp and General Insurance Corp. Life insurance would stay in state hands.
"We will try our best to reverse the opening up of the health insurance sector," Surjeet said.
The CPI-M was also opposed to the government's partial divestment of shares in profitable state-owned firms, he said.
Surjeet warned the United Front against following the liberal economic policies of its predecessor Congress government.
"The United Front is missing one point. In the last election one factor was the economic policies of Congress government which landed them in the soup and a big defeat," Surjeet said.
India began liberalising its economy in 1991 under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's Congress government which opened up trade and industry after decades of socialist control.

Foreign investors complain that the pace of liberalisation is flagging and India needs to take drastic steps to revamp its creaking infrastructure and invite foreign investment if it wants to join the league of the Asian "tiger" economies.
